docs.title: Supercard Workforce Developer Portal
docs.text:
Welcome to the Supercard Workforce Developer Portal, the official documentation for the Supercard Workforce Management API.

This portal provides everything you need to integrate with the platform, including comprehensive REST API documentation, authentication guides, conceptual references, interactive API exploration, and practical integration examples.

Whether you're building HR applications, workforce automation tools, payroll integrations, or reporting dashboards, this documentation will help you quickly understand and integrate with the Supercard Workforce platform.

docs.title: Why Supercard Workforce API?
docs.text:
The Supercard Workforce API enables organizations to automate workforce management through a secure and scalable REST API.

With this API you can:

  • Manage employee information
  • Organize departments
  • Record attendance
  • Manage leave requests
  • Process payroll
  • Generate workforce reports
  • Integrate with HRMS and ERP platforms

The API follows RESTful principles and uses predictable resource-oriented URLs, standard HTTP methods, JSON payloads, and OAuth 2.0 authentication.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The Supercard Workforce Management API uses OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token Authentication to secure access to protected resources.

Every request to a protected endpoint must include a valid access token in the Authorization header.

Authentication ensures that only authorized users and applications can access workforce data while maintaining security, privacy, and compliance.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
The authentication process follows the OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token workflow.

  1. Register your application.
  2. Obtain an OAuth 2.0 access token.
  3. Include the access token in every protected API request.
  4. Receive the API response.
  5. Refresh the token when it expires.
Client Application
        │
        ▼
Request Access Token
        │
        ▼
Authorization Server
        │
        ▼
Access Token
        │
        ▼
Protected API Request
        │
        ▼
Supercard Workforce API

docs.title: Authorization Header
docs.text:
Include the access token in every request.

Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN

Example

GET /employees HTTP/1.1
Host: api.supercard.com
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
Accept: application/json

docs.title: Access Token
docs.text:
An access token represents the authenticated identity of an application or user.

Example

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

Note

The example above is for demonstration purposes only.

docs.title: Token Lifetime
docs.text:
Access tokens are valid for a limited period.

When the token expires, your application must request a new token before accessing protected resources.

Never assume an access token remains valid indefinitely.

docs.title: Example Request
docs.text:
curl --request GET \
  --url https://api.supercard.com/v1/employees \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  --header "Accept: application/json"

docs.title: Successful Response
docs.text:
{
  "success": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "employeeId": 101,
      "firstName": "John",
      "lastName": "Doe"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Common Authentication Errors
docs.text: Status Error Cause Resolution 400 Bad Request Invalid request Verify the request format. 401 Unauthorized Missing or expired token Generate a new access token. 403 Forbidden Insufficient permissions Contact your administrator. 429 Too Many Requests Rate limit exceeded Retry after the specified interval.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these recommendations when integrating with the API.

  • Always use HTTPS.
  • Never expose access tokens in client-side code.
  • Store tokens securely.
  • Rotate credentials regularly.
  • Use the principle of least privilege.
  • Avoid logging sensitive authentication information.
  • Refresh expired tokens before retrying requests.

docs.title: Authentication Checklist
docs.text:
Before making your first API request, verify the following.

  • OAuth 2.0 access token has been generated.
  • Authorization header is included.
  • HTTPS is used.
  • Content-Type is set correctly.
  • Accept header is present.
  • Token has not expired.

docs.title: I receive 401 Unauthorized
docs.text:
Possible causes:

  • Missing Authorization header
  • Invalid token
  • Expired token
  • Incorrect authentication scheme

Recommended actions:

  • Generate a new access token.
  • Verify the Bearer prefix.
  • Confirm the Authorization header is included.
  • Retry the request.

docs.title: I receive 403 Forbidden
docs.text:
Possible causes:

  • User lacks sufficient permissions.
  • Resource access is restricted.

Recommended actions:

  • Verify assigned roles.
  • Contact the system administrator.

docs.title: Do all endpoints require authentication?
docs.text:
Most endpoints require authentication.

Public endpoints, if available, will explicitly state that authentication is not required.

docs.title: Can multiple applications share one access token?
docs.text:
No.

Each application should authenticate independently and manage its own credentials securely.

docs.title: Should access tokens be stored permanently?
docs.text:
No.

Access tokens should be stored securely and refreshed according to your organization's authentication policy.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The Supercard Workforce Management API uses standard HTTP status codes together with structured JSON error responses to help developers quickly identify, diagnose, and resolve issues.

This guide explains how errors are returned, how to interpret them, and recommended troubleshooting practices.

docs.title: Error Response Structure
docs.text:
Whenever a request cannot be processed successfully, the API returns a JSON error response.

Example:

{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "EMPLOYEE_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Employee with ID 101 was not found.",
    "requestId": "REQ-20260730-AB12345",
    "timestamp": "2026-07-30T08:45:18Z"
  }
}

docs.title: Error Response Fields
docs.text: Field Description success Indicates whether the request completed successfully. error.code Machine-readable application error code. error.message Human-readable error description. error.requestId Unique request identifier for troubleshooting. error.timestamp Time when the error occurred (UTC).

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
The API follows standard HTTP status code conventions.

Status Meaning Description 200 OK Success Request completed successfully. 201 Created Resource Created A new resource was created successfully. 204 No Content Success Request succeeded with no response body. 400 Bad Request Client Error Request validation failed. 401 Unauthorized Authentication Error Missing or invalid access token. 403 Forbidden Authorization Error Insufficient permissions. 404 Not Found Resource Error Requested resource does not exist. 409 Conflict Business Rule Error Resource already exists or violates business rules. 422 Unprocessable Entity Validation Error Request syntax is valid but business validation failed. 429 Too Many Requests Rate Limit Too many requests were received. 500 Internal Server Error Server Error Unexpected server-side error. 503 Service Unavailable Service Error API is temporarily unavailable.

docs.title: Common Application Error Codes
docs.text: Error Code Description Recommended Action INVALID_TOKEN Access token is invalid. Generate a new access token. TOKEN_EXPIRED Access token has expired. Refresh or request a new token. EMPLOYEE_NOT_FOUND Employee record does not exist. Verify the employee identifier. DEPARTMENT_NOT_FOUND Department could not be found. Confirm the department ID. DUPLICATE_RESOURCE Resource already exists. Ensure the resource is unique. VALIDATION_ERROR Request validation failed. Review the request payload. RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED Too many requests. Retry after the specified interval. INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR Unexpected server error. Retry later or contact support.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Missing required fields
  • Invalid JSON syntax
  • Incorrect data types
  • Unsupported field values

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Validate the request body.
  • Ensure all required fields are present.
  • Verify JSON syntax.
  • Review endpoint documentation.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Missing Authorization header
  • Invalid Bearer token
  • Expired access token

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Generate a new access token.
  • Include the Authorization header.
  • Verify the Bearer token format.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• User lacks required permissions
  • Resource access restricted

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Verify assigned roles.
  • Contact your system administrator.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Incorrect endpoint URL
  • Invalid resource identifier
  • Resource deleted

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Verify the endpoint URL.
  • Confirm the resource exists.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Duplicate resource
  • Business rule violation

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Review existing resources.
  • Resolve the conflict before retrying.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Business validation failed
  • Invalid field values

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Review validation rules.
  • Correct the request data.
  • Retry the request.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text: • API rate limit exceeded

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Wait for the Retry-After period.
  • Implement exponential backoff.
  • Reduce request frequency.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text: • Unexpected server-side failure

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
• Retry the request.
  • Record the request ID.
  • Contact support if the issue continues.

docs.title: Error Handling Best Practices
docs.text:
To build reliable integrations:

  • Validate requests before sending them.
  • Handle every HTTP status code explicitly.
  • Never ignore error responses.
  • Log the requestId for support investigations.
  • Respect API rate limits.
  • Retry only transient failures.
  • Avoid exposing sensitive error information to end users.

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text: Status Code Retry? Recommendation 400 ❌ Fix the request before retrying. 401 ❌ Generate a new access token. 403 ❌ Verify permissions. 404 ❌ Verify the requested resource. 409 ❌ Resolve the business conflict. 422 ❌ Correct validation errors. 429 ✅ Retry after the specified interval. 500 ✅ Retry after a short delay. 503 ✅ Retry using exponential backoff.

docs.title: Best Practices Checklist
docs.text:
Before contacting support, verify that:

  • OAuth 2.0 access token is valid.
  • Authorization header is present.
  • Request body follows the API schema.
  • Endpoint URL is correct.
  • Resource identifiers are valid.
  • API rate limits have not been exceeded.

Developer Tip

Retry Strategy

Do not automatically retry every failed request.

Retry only transient errors such as 429 Too Many Requests and 503 Service Unavailable. Client-side errors such as 400 Bad Request or 401 Unauthorized require corrective action before retrying.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
docs.text:
This page answers common questions about the Supercard Workforce Management API.

If you're new to the platform, we recommend reading the Getting Started guide before reviewing the FAQs.

docs.title: What is the Supercard Workforce Management API?
docs.text: The Supercard Workforce Management API is a RESTful API that enables applications to integrate with workforce management services such as employee management, attendance tracking, leave management, payroll, and reporting.

docs.title: Who is this API intended for?
docs.text:
The API is designed for:

  • Software Developers
  • Solution Architects
  • HR Technology Teams
  • ERP Integrators
  • System Administrators
  • Technical Partners

docs.title: Which API standard does it follow?
docs.text:
The API follows:

  • REST architecture
  • OpenAPI 3.1 Specification
  • JSON request and response bodies
  • OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token Authentication

docs.title: Do all endpoints require authentication?
docs.text:
Most endpoints require OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token authentication.

If an endpoint is publicly accessible, it will explicitly state that authentication is not required.

docs.title: What authentication method is used?
docs.text:
The API uses OAuth 2.0 Bearer Tokens.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN

docs.title: What should I do if my token expires?
docs.text:
Generate a new access token and retry the request.

Never reuse expired tokens.

docs.title: Which HTTP methods are supported?
docs.text:
The API supports:

  • GET
  • POST
  • PUT
  • DELETE

docs.title: Which data format is supported?
docs.text:
All requests and responses use JSON.

Example:

Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

docs.title: Which date format should I use?
docs.text:
Use the ISO 8601 standard.

Example:

2026-07-30T10:15:30Z

docs.title: How are errors returned?
docs.text:
Errors are returned using a standardized JSON response.

Example:

{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "Required field missing."
  }
}

For more details, see the Error Handling guide.

docs.title: What do HTTP status codes mean?
docs.text:
The API uses standard HTTP status codes.

Common examples include:

Status Meaning 200 Success 201 Resource Created 400 Invalid Request 401 Authentication Failed 404 Resource Not Found 500 Internal Server Error

See the HTTP Status Codes reference for the complete list.

docs.title: Does the API have rate limits?
docs.text:
Yes.

Applications should avoid sending excessive requests and should implement retry logic using exponential backoff.

docs.title: Should I retry failed requests?
docs.text:
Retry only temporary failures such as:

  • 429 Too Many Requests
  • 503 Service Unavailable

Do not automatically retry validation or authentication errors.

docs.title: Is there an official SDK?
docs.text:
This portfolio project does not include official SDK packages.

However, because the API follows the OpenAPI 3.1 specification, SDKs can be generated automatically or implemented using standard HTTP libraries.

docs.title: Can I generate SDKs automatically?
docs.text:
Yes.

The OpenAPI specification can be used with tools such as OpenAPI Generator to generate SDKs for many programming languages.

docs.title: Which API client should I use?
docs.text:
Any HTTP client can be used.

Popular options include:

  • Postman
  • cURL
  • Insomnia
  • Bruno

docs.title: Should I store access tokens in source code?
docs.text:
No.

Always store credentials securely using:

  • Environment variables
  • Secret management solutions
  • Secure credential stores

Never commit secrets to version control.

docs.title: Should I use HTTPS?
docs.text:
Yes.

All API requests should use HTTPS.

docs.title: Attendance API
docs.text:
The Attendance API provides RESTful endpoints for recording, tracking, and reporting employee attendance.

It enables organizations to manage daily attendance records, employee working hours, overtime, attendance summaries, and attendance reports.

The Attendance API integrates with Payroll, Leave Management, and Reporting modules to provide accurate workforce insights.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
An attendance record represents an employee's working activity for a specific day.

Each attendance record contains information such as:

  • Employee information
  • Clock-in time
  • Clock-out time
  • Working hours
  • Break duration
  • Overtime
  • Attendance status
  • Remarks
  • Audit timestamps

All Attendance endpoints require OAuth 2.0 Bearer Authentication.

docs.title: Departments API

The Departments API provides RESTful endpoints for creating, retrieving, updating, and deleting departments within the Supercard Workforce platform.

Departments help organize employees, reporting structures, payroll processing, attendance management, and organizational reporting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A department represents a functional unit within an organization.

Typical examples include:

  • Engineering
  • Human Resources
  • Finance
  • Marketing
  • Sales
  • Operations

Each department contains information such as:

  • Department name
  • Department code
  • Manager
  • Location
  • Budget
  • Employee count
  • Operational status

All Department endpoints require OAuth 2.0 Bearer Authentication.

  • Ensure there are no pending leave requests.
  • Verify attendance records have been processed.
  • Check whether organizational policy requires deactivation instead of deletion.
  • Back up important employee information if required.

  • Log every delete operation for audit purposes.
  • Display a confirmation dialog before deletion.
  • Handle 404 Not Found and 409 Conflict responses gracefully.
  • Never expose this endpoint to unauthorized users.
  • Always use HTTPS.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Deleting employee records is a high-impact operation.

Applications should:

  • Require administrator privileges.
  • Record audit logs for every deletion.
  • Verify user permissions before sending the request.
  • Prevent accidental multiple submissions.
  • Consider implementing multi-factor approval for sensitive environments.

docs.title: Employees API
docs.text:
The Employees API provides RESTful endpoints for creating, retrieving, updating, and deleting employee records within the Supercard Workforce platform.

It is designed for Human Resources (HR) applications, Workforce Management Systems, Payroll platforms, ERP integrations, and custom business applications.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Employee records represent the core entity of the Supercard Workforce API.

Each employee contains information such as:

  • Personal information
  • Contact details
  • Employment details
  • Department assignment
  • Manager information
  • Employment status
  • Salary information
  • Audit timestamps

All employee operations require OAuth 2.0 Bearer Authentication.

docs.title: Leaves API
docs.text:
The Leaves API provides RESTful endpoints for managing employee leave requests throughout their lifecycle.

It enables employees to apply for leave, managers to approve or reject requests, employees to cancel requests when permitted, and HR teams to monitor leave balances and leave history.

The Leaves API integrates with Attendance, Payroll, Employees, and Reporting modules to ensure accurate workforce management.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A leave request represents an employee's request for time away from work.

Each leave request contains information such as:

  • Employee details
  • Leave type
  • Start and end dates
  • Number of leave days
  • Leave reason
  • Approval status
  • Approver information
  • Leave balance
  • Audit timestamps

All Leave endpoints require OAuth 2.0 Bearer Authentication.

This endpoint allows authorized managers and HR administrators to reject leave requests that do not meet organizational policies or business requirements.

docs.title: Payroll API
docs.text:
The Payroll API provides RESTful endpoints for managing employee payroll information within the Supercard Workforce platform.

It enables organizations to process employee salaries, retrieve payroll history, download payslips, and generate salary summaries for payroll administration and financial reporting.

The Payroll API integrates with Attendance, Leave Management, Employees, and Reporting modules to ensure accurate salary calculations and statutory compliance.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A payroll record represents an employee's salary for a specific payroll period.

Each payroll record contains information such as:

  • Employee information
  • Payroll period
  • Gross salary
  • Earnings
  • Deductions
  • Taxes
  • Provident Fund contributions
  • Net salary
  • Payment status
  • Payment date
  • Audit timestamps

All Payroll endpoints require OAuth 2.0 Bearer Authentication.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Error handling is the practice of designing applications to detect, interpret, and respond appropriately to API failures.

A well-designed application should expect failures and recover gracefully whenever possible.

Rather than assuming every request succeeds, developers should anticipate network interruptions, authentication failures, validation errors, rate limits, and temporary service outages.

docs.title: Why Error Handling Matters
docs.text:
API requests can fail for many reasons.

Examples include:

  • Invalid request data
  • Authentication failures
  • Permission issues
  • Network interruptions
  • Rate limiting
  • Temporary service outages
  • Unexpected server errors

Applications that handle these situations correctly provide a more reliable and user-friendly experience.

docs.title: Types of Errors
docs.text: API failures generally fall into two categories.

docs.title: Client Errors (4xx)
docs.text:
Client errors indicate that the request cannot be processed because of an issue with the request itself.

Examples include:

  • Missing required fields
  • Invalid JSON
  • Invalid authentication
  • Insufficient permissions
  • Resource not found

These errors require corrective action before retrying.

docs.title: Server Errors (5xx)
docs.text:
Server errors indicate that the request reached the API successfully, but the server was unable to complete it.

Examples include:

  • Internal server errors
  • Temporary service outages
  • Infrastructure failures

These errors are often temporary and may succeed when retried.

docs.title: Common HTTP Status Codes
docs.text: Status Code Category Recommended Action 200 OK Success Continue processing. 201 Created Success Resource created successfully. 204 No Content Success Operation completed successfully. 400 Bad Request Client Error Correct the request before retrying. 401 Unauthorized Authentication Error Obtain a new access token. 403 Forbidden Authorization Error Verify user permissions. 404 Not Found Resource Error Confirm the requested resource exists. 409 Conflict Business Rule Resolve the conflict before retrying. 422 Unprocessable Entity Validation Error Correct invalid field values. 429 Too Many Requests Rate Limit Retry after the specified delay. 500 Internal Server Error Server Error Retry later. 503 Service Unavailable Service Error Retry using exponential backoff.

docs.title: Error Handling Workflow
docs.text:
Send API Request
        │
        ▼
Receive Response
        │
        ▼
Is Status Code 2xx?
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   │         │
 Yes         No
   │         │
   ▼         ▼
Continue   Identify Error
             │
             ▼
   Is it Recoverable?
         │
    ┌────┴────┐
    │         │
   Yes        No
    │         │
    ▼         ▼
Retry      Log Error
Safely     Notify User

docs.title: Recoverable Errors
docs.text:
These errors are typically temporary.

Examples:

  • HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
  • HTTP 500 Internal Server Error
  • HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
  • Network timeout
  • Temporary connectivity issues

Recommended approach:

  • Retry the request.
  • Use exponential backoff.
  • Respect the Retry-After header.
  • Limit the number of retry attempts.

docs.title: Non-Recoverable Errors
docs.text:
These errors usually require corrective action before another request is made.

Examples:

  • HTTP 400 Bad Request
  • HTTP 401 Unauthorized
  • HTTP 403 Forbidden
  • HTTP 404 Not Found
  • HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity

Recommended approach:

  • Correct the request.
  • Obtain a new access token if required.
  • Validate input data.
  • Retry only after resolving the issue.

docs.title: Logging Best Practices
docs.text:
Applications should log sufficient information to diagnose issues.

Recommended fields include:

  • Request ID
  • Endpoint
  • HTTP method
  • Status code
  • Response time
  • Error code
  • Timestamp

Avoid logging:

  • Access tokens
  • Passwords
  • Personally Identifiable Information (PII)
  • Client secrets

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text:
Not every error should be retried.

Status Code Retry? Recommendation 400 ❌ Correct the request. 401 ❌ Authenticate again. 403 ❌ Verify permissions. 404 ❌ Verify the resource. 409 ❌ Resolve the business conflict. 422 ❌ Correct validation errors. 429 ✅ Retry after the specified delay. 500 ✅ Retry using exponential backoff. 503 ✅ Retry after a short delay.

docs.title: Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
When retrying transient failures, increase the wait time after each unsuccessful attempt.

Example:

Attempt Wait Time 1 1 second 2 2 seconds 3 4 seconds 4 8 seconds 5 16 seconds

Adding a small amount of random delay (known as jitter) helps prevent many clients from retrying at the same time.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
To build resilient integrations:

  • Validate input before sending requests.
  • Handle every documented status code.
  • Retry only transient failures.
  • Log request identifiers.
  • Display meaningful messages to users.
  • Respect API rate limits.
  • Implement request timeouts.
  • Test failure scenarios during development.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid these common implementation issues:

❌ Retrying every failed request.

❌ Ignoring HTTP status codes.

❌ Displaying raw server errors to users.

❌ Logging sensitive credentials.

❌ Assuming network requests never fail.

docs.title: Should every error be retried?
docs.text:
No.

Only retry temporary or recoverable failures such as 429, 500, and 503.

docs.title: Why shouldn't I retry a 400 Bad Request?
docs.text: Because the request itself is invalid. Repeating the same request will produce the same error until the request is corrected.

docs.title: What information should I log?
docs.text:
Log request IDs, endpoints, timestamps, status codes, and response times.

Avoid logging confidential information such as access tokens or passwords.

docs.title: Should users see raw API error messages?
docs.text:
No.

Applications should present user-friendly messages while recording detailed technical information in logs.

Developer Tip

Treat API failures as an expected part of distributed systems. Designing your application to recover gracefully from temporary failures results in a more reliable user experience.

Retry Carefully

Excessive retries can increase server load and worsen outages. Implement retry limits, exponential backoff, and random jitter to ensure responsible API consumption.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Filtering allows you to retrieve only the resources that match specific criteria.

Instead of returning every available record, you can narrow the results using query parameters such as department, employment status, designation, joining date, or location.

Filtering improves performance, reduces network traffic, and helps applications retrieve only the information they need.

docs.title: Why Filtering?
docs.text:
Consider an organization with:

  • 50,000 employees
  • 1,200 departments
  • Millions of attendance records

Returning every record would be inefficient.

Filtering enables your application to retrieve only the relevant subset of data.

Examples include:

  • Employees in Engineering
  • Active employees
  • Employees hired after a specific date
  • Attendance records for a given month
  • Payroll records for a particular pay period

docs.title: How Filtering Works
docs.text:
Filtering is performed using query parameters.

Example:

GET /employees?department=Engineering

The API returns only employees belonging to the Engineering department.

docs.title: Multiple Filters
docs.text:
You can combine multiple filters within a single request.

Example:

GET /employees?department=Engineering&status=Active

The response contains only active employees in the Engineering department.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
Idempotency is the property of an API operation that ensures making the same request multiple times produces the same result as making it once.

It is commonly used to prevent duplicate resource creation when a client retries a request due to network failures, timeouts, or other transient issues.

The Supercard Workforce Management API supports idempotent operations where appropriate to improve reliability and provide a consistent integration experience.

docs.title: Why Idempotency?
docs.text:
Network interruptions and timeouts are common in distributed systems.

Consider the following scenario:

  1. A client submits a request to create a new employee.
  2. The server successfully creates the employee.
  3. The response is lost because of a network interruption.
  4. The client assumes the request failed and retries it.

Without idempotency, the employee could be created twice.

Idempotency prevents duplicate processing by ensuring repeated requests are recognized and handled safely.

docs.title: How Idempotency Works
docs.text:
Clients generate a unique Idempotency Key for each operation that should only be processed once.

The key is included in the request header.

Example:

Idempotency-Key: 7e4c6f0b-d2c3-4d91-9f6d-0c4f7d8b2a91

When the API receives a request:

  1. It checks whether the key has been processed before.
  2. If the key is new, the request is processed normally.
  3. If the same key is received again, the previous result is returned instead of executing the operation a second time.

docs.title: Example Request
docs.text:
POST /employees HTTP/1.1
Host: api.supercard.com
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
Idempotency-Key: 7e4c6f0b-d2c3-4d91-9f6d-0c4f7d8b2a91
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "firstName": "John",
  "lastName": "Doe",
  "department": "Engineering"
}

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "employeeId": 101,
    "firstName": "John",
    "lastName": "Doe"
  }
}

If the same request is sent again with the same Idempotency-Key, the API returns the same response instead of creating another employee.

docs.title: When to Use Idempotency
docs.text:
Idempotency is recommended for operations that create or modify resources.

Typical examples include:

  • Employee creation
  • Leave applications
  • Payroll generation
  • Department creation
  • Report generation

docs.title: HTTP Methods and Idempotency
docs.text:
Not all HTTP methods behave the same way.

HTTP Method Naturally Idempotent Typical Use GET ✅ Yes Retrieve resources PUT ✅ Yes Replace an existing resource DELETE ✅ Yes Remove a resource POST ❌ No Create a new resource PATCH ❌ Usually No Partially update a resource

Because POST requests often create new resources, they benefit the most from idempotency keys.

docs.title: Idempotency Workflow
docs.text:
Client
   │
   │ POST /employees
   │ Idempotency-Key: abc123
   ▼
API Server
   │
   ├── Key not seen before
   │       │
   │       ▼
   │   Create Employee
   │       │
   │       ▼
   │ Return Success
   │
   └── Same key received again
           │
           ▼
   Return Previous Response

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these recommendations when implementing idempotent requests.

  • Generate a new idempotency key for each new operation.
  • Reuse the same key only when retrying the same request.
  • Use UUIDs or other globally unique identifiers.
  • Store keys securely until the request completes.
  • Ensure the request body remains unchanged when retrying.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid the following mistakes:

❌ Reusing the same key for different operations.

❌ Changing the request payload while using the same key.

❌ Generating predictable or sequential keys.

❌ Assuming all endpoints support idempotency.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
When using idempotency keys:

  • Generate cryptographically strong unique identifiers.
  • Do not expose sensitive information within the key.
  • Treat idempotency keys as request metadata rather than authentication credentials.
  • Continue to use HTTPS for all API requests.

docs.title: Why isn't POST naturally idempotent?
docs.text: A POST request typically creates a new resource each time it is processed. Without an idempotency mechanism, retrying the same POST request may create duplicate resources.

docs.title: Can I reuse an idempotency key?
docs.text:
Only when retrying the exact same request.

A different operation must always use a new key.

docs.title: Does every endpoint support idempotency?
docs.text:
No.

Refer to the endpoint documentation to determine whether idempotency keys are supported.

docs.title: How long should an idempotency key remain valid?
docs.text: The retention period depends on the API implementation. Clients should assume keys are temporary and generate a new key for each new operation.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text:
Continue learning:

  • Versioning
  • Rate Limiting
  • Error Handling
  • Authentication
  • Create Employee

Developer Tip

Generate a UUID for every idempotent request. Reuse the same UUID only if you need to retry that exact request after a timeout or network failure.

Duplicate Operations

Changing the request body while reusing the same idempotency key can produce unexpected results or validation errors. Always retry with the identical request payload.

Portfolio Project

The idempotency examples shown in this documentation demonstrate common enterprise REST API design practices. Support for idempotency keys varies between APIs and should be documented for each applicable endpoint.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Pagination is a technique used to divide large collections of resources into smaller, manageable sets called pages.

Instead of returning thousands of records in a single response, the Supercard Workforce Management API returns only a subset of records for each request. This improves performance, reduces bandwidth consumption, and provides a better developer experience.

docs.title: Why Pagination?
docs.text:
Imagine an organization with:

  • 50,000 employees
  • 500 departments
  • Millions of attendance records

Returning all records in a single API response would:

  • Increase response time
  • Consume excessive network bandwidth
  • Increase memory usage
  • Slow down client applications
  • Impact server performance

Pagination solves these problems by returning results in smaller batches.

docs.title: How Pagination Works
docs.text:
The Supercard Workforce API supports pagination using query parameters.

Typical parameters include:

Parameter Description Default page Page number to retrieve 1 limit Number of records per page 25

Example:

GET /employees?page=2&limit=25

This request retrieves:

  • Page 2
  • 25 employee records

docs.title: Example Request
docs.text:
curl --request GET \
  --url "https://api.supercard.com/v1/employees?page=2&limit=25" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN"

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "success": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "employeeId": 126,
      "firstName": "John",
      "lastName": "Doe"
    }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "page": 2,
    "limit": 25,
    "totalRecords": 512,
    "totalPages": 21,
    "hasNextPage": true,
    "hasPreviousPage": true
  }
}

docs.title: Pagination Fields
docs.text: Field Description page Current page number limit Number of records returned totalRecords Total number of available records totalPages Total number of available pages hasNextPage Indicates whether another page exists hasPreviousPage Indicates whether a previous page exists

docs.title: Pagination Workflow
docs.text:
Request Page 1
        │
        ▼
Receive 25 Records
        │
        ▼
Need More Results?
        │
      Yes
        │
        ▼
Request Page 2
        │
        ▼
Receive Next 25 Records
        │
        ▼
Continue Until hasNextPage = false

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these recommendations when working with paginated endpoints.

  • Use the default page size unless a larger page is required.
  • Request only the data your application needs.
  • Check the hasNextPage field before requesting another page.
  • Avoid requesting extremely large page sizes.
  • Cache responses where appropriate.
  • Combine pagination with filtering and sorting for better performance.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid the following mistakes:

❌ Requesting every page simultaneously.

❌ Ignoring pagination metadata.

❌ Using excessively large page sizes.

❌ Assuming the total number of pages never changes.

docs.title: Combining Pagination with Filtering
docs.text:
Pagination works seamlessly with filtering.

Example:

GET /employees?department=Engineering&page=1&limit=20

docs.title: Combining Pagination with Sorting
docs.text:
Pagination can also be combined with sorting.

Example:

GET /employees?sort=lastName&page=3&limit=20

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
For optimal performance:

  • Keep page sizes reasonable.
  • Retrieve only required fields where supported.
  • Cache frequently requested pages.
  • Avoid unnecessary repeated requests.
  • Respect API rate limits.

docs.title: Can I request all records at once?
docs.text:
No.

Large datasets should always be retrieved using pagination.

docs.title: Can pagination metadata change?
docs.text:
Yes.

If resources are created or deleted while paging through results, values such as totalPages and totalRecords may change.

docs.title: What happens if I request a page that doesn't exist?
docs.text: The API returns an appropriate HTTP error response indicating that the requested page is outside the available range.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text:
Continue learning:

  • Filtering
  • Sorting
  • Rate Limiting
  • Versioning
  • Employees API

Developer Tip

Use pagination metadata such as hasNextPage rather than calculating page counts manually. This makes client applications more resilient to changes in the underlying data.

Performance

Avoid requesting unnecessarily large page sizes. Smaller, predictable responses improve performance for both clients and servers.

Portfolio Project

The pagination examples shown in this documentation are representative of common REST API design patterns and are provided to demonstrate enterprise API documentation practices.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Rate limiting controls the number of API requests that a client can make within a specified time period.

It protects the API from excessive traffic, ensures fair usage among consumers, and maintains consistent performance for all applications.

If a client exceeds the permitted request limit, the API returns an HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response.

docs.title: Why Rate Limiting?
docs.text:
Without rate limiting, a single client could overwhelm the API by sending an excessive number of requests.

Rate limiting helps to:

  • Protect server resources
  • Maintain API availability
  • Prevent abuse and denial-of-service attacks
  • Ensure fair access for all API consumers
  • Improve overall platform stability

docs.title: How Rate Limiting Works
docs.text:
Each client is allowed a maximum number of requests during a predefined time window.

Example policy:

Limit Time Window 100 requests 1 minute

If the limit is exceeded before the time window resets, additional requests are temporarily rejected.

docs.title: Example Request
docs.text:
GET /employees HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN

docs.title: Successful Response
docs.text: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

docs.title: Rate Limit Exceeded
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

Example response:

{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
    "message": "Request limit exceeded. Please retry later."
  }
}

docs.title: Rate Limit Headers
docs.text:
Many APIs provide additional response headers to help clients manage request limits.

Example:

X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 27
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1722326400
Retry-After: 60
Header Description X-RateLimit-Limit Maximum requests allowed during the window X-RateLimit-Remaining Remaining requests before the limit is reached X-RateLimit-Reset Time when the limit resets Retry-After Number of seconds to wait before retrying

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text:
When the API returns 429 Too Many Requests, your application should:

  1. Stop sending requests immediately.
  2. Read the Retry-After header.
  3. Wait for the specified duration.
  4. Retry the request.

Avoid continuously retrying failed requests, as this can prolong the rate limit.

docs.title: Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
For temporary failures such as 429 or 503, implement exponential backoff.

Example retry delays:

Attempt Delay 1 1 second 2 2 seconds 3 4 seconds 4 8 seconds 5 16 seconds

This strategy reduces load on the API while increasing the likelihood of a successful retry.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these recommendations when integrating with rate-limited endpoints.

  • Cache responses whenever appropriate.
  • Avoid polling the API unnecessarily.
  • Batch requests where supported.
  • Use pagination instead of requesting large datasets.
  • Respect the Retry-After header.
  • Implement exponential backoff.
  • Monitor request usage in production.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid these common mistakes:

❌ Ignoring HTTP 429 responses.

❌ Retrying requests immediately.

❌ Sending duplicate requests in parallel.

❌ Polling the API too frequently.

❌ Ignoring response headers.

docs.title: Monitoring Rate Limits
docs.text:
Applications should monitor:

  • Requests per minute
  • Remaining request quota
  • Retry attempts
  • Failed requests
  • Average response time

Monitoring these metrics helps identify bottlenecks before they affect users.

docs.title: Why am I receiving HTTP 429?
docs.text: Your application has exceeded the permitted request limit for the current time window.

docs.title: Should I retry immediately?
docs.text:
No.

Wait for the duration specified in the Retry-After header before sending another request.

docs.title: Can rate limits change?
docs.text:
Yes.

Rate limits may vary depending on the API plan, endpoint, or organizational policy.

Always refer to the latest API documentation.

docs.title: Do all endpoints have the same rate limit?
docs.text:
Not necessarily.

Some endpoints may enforce different limits based on resource usage or business requirements.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text:
Continue learning:

  • Pagination
  • Filtering
  • Sorting
  • Versioning
  • Error Handling

Developer Tip

Design your application to gracefully handle HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses. A well-implemented retry strategy improves reliability without overwhelming the API.

Avoid Retry Storms

If many clients retry requests simultaneously after a rate limit is reached, the API may become overloaded. Use exponential backoff and add random jitter to distribute retry attempts over time.

Portfolio Project

The rate limiting values, response headers, and retry examples shown in this documentation are representative examples designed to demonstrate enterprise REST API documentation practices. Actual limits depend on deployment and operational policies.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
Sorting allows you to organize API responses in a predictable order based on one or more resource attributes.

Instead of receiving records in the default order, you can specify how results should be arranged—for example, alphabetically by employee name, chronologically by joining date, or numerically by salary.

Sorting improves data presentation, simplifies client-side processing, and helps users quickly locate relevant information.

docs.title: Why Sorting?
docs.text:
Consider the following scenarios:

  • Display employees alphabetically.
  • Show the newest employees first.
  • View the highest salaries at the top.
  • List attendance records by date.
  • Display payroll history from the latest payroll cycle.

Without sorting, applications would need to process and reorder data after receiving it, increasing complexity and reducing performance.

docs.title: How Sorting Works
docs.text:
Sorting is performed using query parameters.

Example:

GET /employees?sort=lastName

The response returns employees sorted alphabetically by last name.

docs.title: Sort Direction
docs.text:
Most endpoints support both ascending and descending order.

Direction Description asc Ascending order (default) desc Descending order

Example:

GET /employees?sort=lastName&order=asc

Descending order:

GET /employees?sort=joiningDate&order=desc

docs.title: Sort Employees by Last Name
docs.text: GET /employees?sort=lastName

docs.title: Sort by Joining Date (Newest First)
docs.text: GET /employees?sort=joiningDate&order=desc

docs.title: Sort by Salary
docs.text: GET /employees?sort=salary&order=desc

docs.title: Sort Attendance by Date
docs.text: GET /attendance?sort=attendanceDate&order=desc

docs.title: Sort Payroll by Payroll Period
docs.text: GET /payroll?sort=payPeriod&order=desc

docs.title: Example cURL Request
docs.text:
curl --request GET \
  --url "https://api.supercard.com/v1/employees?sort=joiningDate&order=desc" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN"

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "success": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "employeeId": 205,
      "firstName": "Jane",
      "lastName": "Smith",
      "joiningDate": "2026-06-15"
    },
    {
      "employeeId": 182,
      "firstName": "John",
      "lastName": "Doe",
      "joiningDate": "2026-05-28"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Common Sort Fields
docs.text:
Field Description firstName Employee first name lastName Employee last name joiningDate Employee joining date salary Employee salary department Department name attendanceDate Attendance date payPeriod Payroll period

Note: Supported sort fields vary by endpoint. Refer to the endpoint documentation for the complete list of supported fields.

docs.title: Combining Sorting with Filtering
docs.text:
Sorting and filtering are commonly used together.

Example:

GET /employees?department=Engineering&sort=lastName

This request returns Engineering employees sorted alphabetically by last name.

docs.title: Combining Sorting with Pagination
docs.text:
Sorting also works with pagination.

Example:

GET /employees?sort=joiningDate&order=desc&page=2&limit=20

This retrieves the second page of employees sorted by joining date in descending order.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these recommendations when using sorting.

  • Sort only on supported fields.
  • Choose a sort order that matches the user experience.
  • Combine sorting with filtering to reduce unnecessary processing.
  • Use pagination when sorting large datasets.
  • Maintain consistent sorting across related API requests.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid the following mistakes:

❌ Sorting by unsupported fields.

❌ Assuming every endpoint supports identical sort options.

❌ Sorting large datasets without pagination.

❌ Relying on the API's default ordering.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Sorting large datasets may increase processing time.

For optimal performance:

  • Filter data before sorting whenever possible.
  • Request only the records you need.
  • Combine sorting with pagination.
  • Avoid repeatedly requesting the same sorted data if caching is appropriate.

docs.title: Can I sort by multiple fields?
docs.text:
Some endpoints may support multi-field sorting.

Example:

GET /employees?sort=department,lastName

Refer to the endpoint documentation to determine whether multi-field sorting is supported.

docs.title: What happens if I specify an unsupported field?
docs.text: The API returns a validation error indicating that the requested sort field is not supported.

docs.title: Is ascending order the default?
docs.text:
Yes.

If no sort direction is provided, results are typically returned in ascending order unless otherwise documented.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text:
Continue learning:

  • Pagination
  • Filtering
  • Rate Limiting
  • Versioning
  • Employees API

Developer Tip

Always specify both the sort field and the sort direction explicitly. This makes your application behavior predictable and avoids relying on default API behavior.

Performance

Sorting large datasets without pagination can increase response times and resource usage. Combine sorting with pagination for the best performance.

Portfolio Project

The sorting examples shown in this documentation are representative examples designed to demonstrate enterprise REST API documentation practices. Supported sort fields and query parameters may vary between endpoints.

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
API versioning is the practice of managing changes to an API while maintaining compatibility for existing client applications.

As APIs evolve, new features are added, existing functionality is improved, and occasionally breaking changes become necessary. Versioning enables these changes without disrupting applications that rely on previous API behavior.

The Supercard Workforce Management API uses URI-based versioning to provide a stable and predictable integration experience.

docs.title: Why Versioning?
docs.text:
Applications often integrate with an API for many years.

If breaking changes were introduced without versioning:

  • Existing integrations could stop working.
  • Client applications would require immediate updates.
  • Production systems could experience unexpected failures.
  • Developers would lose confidence in API stability.

Versioning allows new functionality to be introduced while preserving backward compatibility for existing consumers.

docs.title: Versioning Strategy
docs.text:
The Supercard Workforce Management API uses URI-based versioning.

Example:

https://api.supercard.com/v1/employees

In this example:

  • v1 represents Version 1 of the API.
  • Future releases may introduce v2, v3, and so on.

docs.title: Why URI Versioning?
docs.text:
URI versioning is:

  • Simple to understand
  • Easy to document
  • Visible in every request
  • Supported by all HTTP clients
  • Widely adopted across REST APIs

For portfolio purposes, URI versioning clearly communicates the version being used.

docs.title: Common Versioning Strategies
docs.text:
Several versioning strategies are used across the industry.

Strategy Example Advantages Considerations URI Versioning /v1/employees Easy to understand and document Requires new endpoint paths Header Versioning API-Version: 1 Clean URLs Less visible and harder to test manually Query Parameter ?version=1 Easy to implement Less common for REST APIs Content Negotiation Accept: application/vnd.company.v1+json Flexible and standards-based More complex to configure

The Supercard Workforce API uses URI Versioning.

docs.title: Example Requests
docs.text:
Version 1

GET https://api.supercard.com/v1/employees

Future Version

GET https://api.supercard.com/v2/employees

Applications should explicitly target the version they support.

docs.title: Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
Whenever possible, new functionality should be introduced without breaking existing integrations.

Examples of backward-compatible changes include:

  • Adding optional request parameters
  • Introducing new response fields
  • Adding new endpoints
  • Improving documentation

These changes allow existing applications to continue functioning without modification.

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text:
Breaking changes require a new major API version.

Examples include:

  • Removing endpoints
  • Renaming request parameters
  • Changing response formats
  • Modifying authentication requirements
  • Changing validation rules
  • Altering resource identifiers

Applications using an older version should continue to function until that version reaches end-of-life.

docs.title: Deprecation Policy
docs.text:
Before removing or replacing an API version:

  1. Announce the deprecation.
  2. Provide migration guidance.
  3. Continue supporting the previous version during the transition period.
  4. Publish an end-of-support date.
  5. Remove the deprecated version after the announced deadline.

This approach gives developers sufficient time to update their applications.

docs.title: Migration Best Practices
docs.text:
When upgrading to a newer API version:

  • Review the release notes.
  • Read the migration guide.
  • Test integrations in a non-production environment.
  • Validate request and response formats.
  • Update automated tests.
  • Deploy gradually using a staged rollout.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Follow these recommendations when integrating with versioned APIs.

  • Always specify the API version explicitly.
  • Avoid relying on undocumented behavior.
  • Monitor release notes for upcoming changes.
  • Plan for version upgrades during regular maintenance.
  • Test integrations before adopting a new version.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid the following mistakes:

❌ Omitting the API version.

❌ Assuming future versions are backward compatible.

❌ Upgrading directly in production without testing.

❌ Ignoring deprecation announcements.

❌ Hardcoding undocumented behavior.

docs.title: Why can't the API change without versioning?
docs.text: Because existing applications depend on stable behavior. Versioning allows improvements without breaking current integrations.

docs.title: Will Version 1 always be supported?
docs.text:
Not indefinitely.

Older versions may eventually be deprecated. Deprecation schedules and migration guidance are communicated through release notes and documentation.

docs.title: Should I always use the latest version?
docs.text:
For new integrations, yes.

Existing applications should upgrade after reviewing the release notes and validating compatibility.

docs.title: What happens if I call an unsupported version?
docs.text: The API typically returns an error indicating that the requested version is unavailable or no longer supported.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text:
Continue learning:

  • Pagination
  • Filtering
  • Sorting
  • Rate Limiting
  • Error Handling

Developer Tip

Pin your application to a specific API version rather than relying on the latest available version. This ensures predictable behavior and reduces the risk of unexpected breaking changes.

Breaking Changes

Never upgrade directly to a new major API version in production without validating your application against the updated API. Always test changes in a development or staging environment first.

Portfolio Project

The versioning strategy described in this documentation is intended to demonstrate enterprise REST API design principles. Version numbers, URLs, and migration examples are illustrative and do not represent a live production API.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Webhooks enable applications to receive real-time notifications when specific events occur.

Instead of repeatedly polling the API to check for changes, a webhook allows the API to automatically send an HTTP request to a client-defined endpoint whenever an event is triggered.

Although the current version of the Supercard Workforce Management API does not provide webhook support, understanding webhook concepts is important for designing scalable, event-driven integrations.

docs.title: Why Webhooks?
docs.text:
Without webhooks, applications often poll the API at regular intervals.

Example:

Every 30 seconds:

GET /employees
GET /attendance
GET /leave-requests

Polling has several disadvantages:

  • Unnecessary API requests
  • Increased network traffic
  • Higher server load
  • Delayed updates
  • Increased rate-limit usage

Webhooks eliminate these problems by notifying applications only when relevant events occur.

docs.title: Polling vs Webhooks
docs.text: Polling Webhooks Client requests updates repeatedly Server sends updates automatically Increased API traffic Reduced API traffic Delayed event detection Near real-time notifications Higher infrastructure cost More efficient resource usage Consumes rate limits Minimal API requests

docs.title: How Webhooks Work
docs.text:
A typical webhook workflow consists of four steps.

  1. The client registers a webhook endpoint.
  2. An event occurs within the platform.
  3. The API sends an HTTP POST request to the registered endpoint.
  4. The client processes the event.

Example workflow:

Employee Created
        │
        ▼
Supercard Workforce API
        │
        ▼
HTTP POST
        │
        ▼
https://example.com/webhooks
        │
        ▼
Client Processes Event

docs.title: Example Webhook Event
docs.text:
A webhook payload is typically sent as JSON.

{
  "event": "employee.created",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-30T10:15:30Z",
  "data": {
    "employeeId": 101,
    "firstName": "John",
    "lastName": "Doe"
  }
}

docs.title: Common Webhook Events
docs.text:
Future versions of the API may provide events such as:

Event Description employee.created New employee added employee.updated Employee information updated employee.deleted Employee removed attendance.clocked-in Employee clocked in attendance.clocked-out Employee clocked out leave.approved Leave request approved leave.rejected Leave request rejected payroll.generated Payroll processing completed

docs.title: Webhook Delivery
docs.text:
When a webhook is triggered:

  1. The API sends an HTTP POST request.
  2. The client returns an HTTP 2xx response.
  3. The delivery is considered successful.

If the client returns a non-success status code, the API may retry delivery depending on the implementation.

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
Webhook endpoints should be secured.

Recommended practices include:

  • Use HTTPS.
  • Validate webhook signatures.
  • Verify request authenticity.
  • Ignore duplicate events.
  • Respond quickly.
  • Process events asynchronously.
  • Log delivery failures.

docs.title: Handling Duplicate Events
docs.text:
Webhook deliveries are often designed to be at least once rather than exactly once.

Applications should therefore:

  • Treat events as idempotent.
  • Ignore duplicate event identifiers.
  • Process the same event safely if delivered more than once.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
When designing webhook consumers:

  • Respond with HTTP 200 as quickly as possible.
  • Perform long-running work asynchronously.
  • Store event identifiers.
  • Validate every payload.
  • Implement retry handling.
  • Monitor failed deliveries.
  • Log webhook activity.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid the following:

❌ Trusting every incoming request.

❌ Processing events synchronously.

❌ Ignoring duplicate deliveries.

❌ Returning slow responses.

❌ Not validating webhook signatures.

docs.title: Why use webhooks instead of polling?
docs.text: Webhooks reduce unnecessary API requests and provide near real-time updates.

docs.title: Do webhooks replace REST APIs?
docs.text:
No.

REST APIs remain the primary mechanism for requesting and modifying resources.

Webhooks notify applications that something has changed.

docs.title: Are webhooks guaranteed to be delivered exactly once?
docs.text:
Not necessarily.

Applications should be designed to safely process duplicate deliveries.

docs.title: Does the current API support webhooks?
docs.text:
No.

Webhook support is not included in the current version of this portfolio project.

This page explains the concept and illustrates how webhook functionality could be incorporated into a future release.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text:
Continue learning:

  • Authentication
  • Idempotency
  • Error Handling
  • Rate Limiting

Developer Tip

Design webhook consumers to be idempotent. Processing the same event more than once should not create duplicate records or inconsistent application state.

Security

Never trust incoming webhook requests by default. Always validate the request source, verify signatures when available, and use HTTPS for all webhook endpoints.

Portfolio Project

The current version of the Supercard Workforce Management API does not implement webhook functionality. This page demonstrates enterprise documentation practices by explaining webhook concepts and illustrating how event-driven integrations could be supported in future versions.

docs.title: Date and Time Formats
docs.text:
Reference Guide

The Supercard Workforce API uses standardized date and time formats based on the ISO 8601 international standard. Using a consistent format ensures interoperability between clients, servers, and third-party integrations.

Unless otherwise specified, all timestamps are represented in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).

docs.title: Why Standardized Date Formats?
docs.text:
Different regions represent dates differently.

For example:

Format Interpretation 01/02/2025 January 2 or February 1? 02-01-2025 Ambiguous 2025-02-01 Unambiguous (ISO 8601)

To eliminate ambiguity, the Supercard Workforce API always uses ISO 8601 formats.

docs.title: Date Format
docs.text:
Dates without a time component use:

YYYY-MM-DD

Example:

2025-02-06

Used for:

  • Joining dates
  • Leave dates
  • Payroll periods
  • Attendance dates
  • Birth dates

docs.title: Date-Time Format
docs.text:
Date and time values use:

YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ssZ

Example:

2025-02-06T15:30:45Z

Meaning:

Component Value Date 2025-02-06 Time 15:30:45 Time Zone UTC (Z)

docs.title: UTC Time
docs.text:
The API stores and returns timestamps in UTC.

Example:

2025-02-06T15:30:45Z

The suffix:

Z

indicates Zulu Time (UTC).

Clients may convert UTC timestamps to local time zones for display.

docs.title: Employee Joining Date
docs.text:
{
  "joiningDate": "2025-02-01"
}

docs.title: Attendance Timestamp
docs.text:
{
  "clockInTime": "2025-02-06T09:02:14Z",
  "clockOutTime": "2025-02-06T18:01:53Z"
}

docs.title: Payroll Period
docs.text:
Payroll periods use the following format:

YYYY-MM

Example:

2025-02

Represents:

February 2025

docs.title: Query Parameter Examples
docs.text:
Retrieve attendance records.

GET /v1/attendance?fromDate=2025-02-01&toDate=2025-02-28

Generate payroll.

GET /v1/payroll/history?payrollPeriod=2025-02

docs.title: Date Validation
docs.text:
Examples of valid dates:

2025-01-31
2025-12-25
2026-03-01

Invalid examples:

31/01/2025
01-31-2025
2025/01/31
January 31, 2025

docs.title: Leap Years
docs.text:
The API follows the Gregorian calendar.

Valid:

2024-02-29

Invalid:

docs.title: Time Zone Conversion
docs.text:
Although responses are returned in UTC, clients may display them in local time.

Example:

UTC:

2025-02-06T12:00:00Z

India Standard Time (UTC+05:30):

2025-02-06T17:30:00+05:30

The API itself always stores and returns UTC values.

docs.title: Milliseconds
docs.text:
Most responses omit milliseconds.

Standard format:

2025-02-06T15:30:45Z

Some future endpoints may include fractional seconds when higher precision is required.

Example:

2025-02-06T15:30:45.123Z

Applications should be prepared to accept both formats.

docs.title: Date and Time Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR

A[Client Sends Date]

A --> B[API Validates Format]

B --> C[Convert to UTC]

C --> D[Store Data]

D --> E[Return ISO 8601 Response]

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always use ISO 8601 formats.
  • Send dates in UTC whenever possible.
  • Convert timestamps to local time only for display.
  • Validate date formats before sending requests.
  • Use four-digit years.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using locale-specific formats such as 31/01/2025.

❌ Omitting the time zone from timestamps.

❌ Assuming timestamps are returned in the client's local time.

❌ Using text-based month names.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Consistent date handling helps:

  • Improve audit accuracy.
  • Simplify distributed system logging.
  • Prevent time zone inconsistencies.
  • Support compliance reporting.

Store UTC

Store timestamps in UTC and convert them to the user's local time only when displaying information.

ISO 8601 Standard

Every date and timestamp returned by the Supercard Workforce API follows the ISO 8601 international standard unless explicitly documented otherwise.

Time Zone Awareness

Do not assume timestamps are returned in your local time zone. All API timestamps are expressed in UTC.

docs.title: Error Codes
docs.text:
Reference Guide

The Supercard Workforce API returns standardized application error codes for every failed request. These codes are stable identifiers intended for programmatic error handling and troubleshooting.

Each error response contains:

  • An HTTP status code
  • A machine-readable error code
  • A human-readable error message
  • Request metadata

Applications should rely on error.code rather than parsing error messages.

docs.title: Standard Error Response
docs.text:
{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "The requested employee could not be found."
  },
  "meta": {
    "requestId": "REQ-10001",
    "correlationId": "CORR-7C41A9F3",
    "timestamp": "2025-02-06T14:00:00Z",
    "apiVersion": "v1"
  }
}

docs.title: Error Categories
docs.text: Category Description Validation Invalid request data Authentication Invalid or missing credentials Authorization Insufficient permissions Resource Missing or duplicate resources Business Rules Domain-specific validation failures Rate Limiting Request quota exceeded Server Unexpected server errors

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description INVALID_REQUEST 400 Request syntax is invalid. INVALID_PARAMETER 400 One or more request parameters are invalid. INVALID_FILTER 400 Invalid filter parameter supplied. INVALID_SORT_FIELD 400 Unsupported sorting field. INVALID_PAGINATION 400 Invalid pagination values. VALIDATION_FAILED 422 Request validation failed. REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING 422 Required field is missing. INVALID_DATE_RANGE 422 The specified date range is invalid.

docs.title: Authentication Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description AUTHENTICATION_FAILED 401 Authentication credentials are invalid. ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRED 401 Access token has expired. INVALID_ACCESS_TOKEN 401 Access token is invalid. MISSING_ACCESS_TOKEN 401 Access token is missing.

docs.title: Authorization Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description ACCESS_DENIED 403 Insufficient permissions. INSUFFICIENT_ROLE 403 User role cannot perform this action. ORGANIZATION_ACCESS_DENIED 403 Access outside organization scope is not permitted.

docs.title: Resource Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND 404 Requested resource does not exist. EMPLOYEE_NOT_FOUND 404 Employee not found. DEPARTMENT_NOT_FOUND 404 Department not found. ATTENDANCE_NOT_FOUND 404 Attendance record not found. LEAVE_REQUEST_NOT_FOUND 404 Leave request not found. PAYROLL_NOT_FOUND 404 Payroll record not found.

docs.title: Conflict Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description DUPLICATE_RESOURCE 409 Resource already exists. DUPLICATE_EMAIL 409 Employee email already exists. IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT 409 Idempotency key reused with different request. RESOURCE_ALREADY_EXISTS 409 Resource already exists.

docs.title: Business Rule Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description INSUFFICIENT_LEAVE_BALANCE 422 Leave balance is insufficient. INVALID_PAYROLL_PERIOD 422 Payroll period is invalid. PAYROLL_ALREADY_GENERATED 409 Payroll has already been generated. CLOCK_IN_ALREADY_EXISTS 409 Employee has already clocked in. CLOCK_OUT_NOT_ALLOWED 422 Clock-out request is not allowed. INVALID_EMPLOYMENT_STATUS 422 Employee status is invalid for this operation.

docs.title: Report Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description REPORT_GENERATION_FAILED 500 Report generation failed. REPORT_NOT_FOUND 404 Requested report not found. UNSUPPORTED_EXPORT_FORMAT 422 Requested export format is not supported. EXPORT_JOB_EXPIRED 404 Export job has expired.

docs.title: Rate Limiting Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429 Request limit exceeded.

docs.title: Server Errors
docs.text: Error Code HTTP Status Description INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR 500 Unexpected server error. SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE 503 Service is temporarily unavailable. DATABASE_ERROR 500 Database operation failed. TIMEOUT 504 Request timed out.

docs.title: Example Validation Error
docs.text:
{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
    "message": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
    "details": [
      {
        "field": "email",
        "message": "A valid email address is required."
      }
    ]
  },
  "meta": {
    "requestId": "REQ-10002",
    "correlationId": "CORR-7C41A9F3",
    "timestamp": "2025-02-06T14:10:00Z",
    "apiVersion": "v1"
  }
}

docs.title: Example Authentication Error
docs.text:
{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRED",
    "message": "Your access token has expired."
  },
  "meta": {
    "requestId": "REQ-10003",
    "correlationId": "CORR-7C41A9F3",
    "timestamp": "2025-02-06T14:15:00Z",
    "apiVersion": "v1"
  }
}

docs.title: Error Handling Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TD

A[Client Request]

A --> B{Valid Request?}

B -->|No| C[Return Validation Error]

B -->|Yes| D{Authenticated?}

D -->|No| E[Return Authentication Error]

D -->|Yes| F{Authorized?}

F -->|No| G[Return Authorization Error]

F -->|Yes| H{Business Rules Valid?}

H -->|No| I[Return Business Rule Error]

H -->|Yes| J[Process Request]

J --> K[Success]

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use error.code for application logic.
  • Display user-friendly error messages in the UI.
  • Log requestId and correlationId.
  • Retry only when appropriate.
  • Validate user input before sending requests.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Parsing the error message instead of using error.code.

❌ Ignoring the HTTP status code.

❌ Retrying validation errors.

❌ Displaying internal server errors directly to end users.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
The API never exposes:

  • Passwords
  • Access tokens
  • SQL queries
  • Database schemas
  • Stack traces
  • Internal implementation details

This protects the platform against information disclosure.

Build Around Error Codes

Error messages may change for clarity or localization, but error.code values remain stable and should be used for application logic.

Consistent Across the API

Every endpoint returns errors using the same response structure and standardized error codes described in this reference.

Retry Carefully

Only retry temporary failures such as RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED or SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE. Validation and authorization errors require corrective action before retrying.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Reference Guide

This glossary defines common terms, acronyms, and concepts used throughout the Supercard Workforce API documentation.

The glossary provides a single source of truth for technical, HR, payroll, attendance, authentication, and API terminology.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Application Programming Interface.

A collection of endpoints that allow client applications to communicate with the Supercard Workforce platform.

docs.title: API Version
docs.text:
A numbered release of the API.

Example:

/v1/employees

docs.title: Access Token
docs.text:
A temporary credential issued after successful authentication.

Access tokens are sent using the Authorization header.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN

docs.title: Attendance Record
docs.text: A record containing an employee's clock-in, clock-out, working hours, and attendance status.

docs.title: Bearer Token
docs.text: An OAuth 2.0 access token transmitted using the HTTP Authorization header.

docs.title: Business Rules
docs.text:
Application-specific rules that determine whether a request is permitted.

Example:

  • Leave balance must be sufficient.
  • Payroll cannot be generated twice for the same period.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
An application that communicates with the Supercard Workforce API.

Examples:

  • Web application
  • Mobile application
  • HR portal
  • Third-party integration

docs.title: Correlation ID
docs.text:
A client-generated identifier used to trace a request across multiple services.

Example:

X-Correlation-ID

docs.title: Department
docs.text:
An organizational unit that groups employees.

Examples:

  • Finance
  • Human Resources
  • Marketing

docs.text: The process of marking an API version or feature for future removal while continuing to support it for a limited period.

docs.title: Employee
docs.text: A workforce member managed within the Supercard Workforce system.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
A URL representing a specific API operation.

Example:

docs.title: Export Job
docs.text: An asynchronous task responsible for generating downloadable reports.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
Hypertext Transfer Protocol

The communication protocol used by the API.

docs.title: HTTP Status Code
docs.text:
A standardized response indicating the result of an HTTP request.

Examples:

  • 200 OK
  • 404 Not Found
  • 500 Internal Server Error

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
A property that allows the same request to be safely repeated without causing duplicate operations.

Idempotency-Key

docs.title: ISO 8601
docs.text:
The international standard used for dates and timestamps.

2025-02-06T15:30:45Z

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:

The data format used for nearly all request and response payloads.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Supplementary information describing a response.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
The authentication framework used by the Supercard Workforce API.

A technique for splitting large collections into smaller pages.

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
HTTP headers provide additional information about an API request or response.

The Supercard Workforce Management API uses standard HTTP headers for authentication, content negotiation, request tracing, caching, and rate limiting.

This guide describes the headers commonly used when interacting with the API.

docs.title: Request Headers
docs.text: Clients send request headers to provide authentication credentials, specify accepted content types, and communicate request metadata.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Authenticates the request using an OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN

Required for all protected endpoints.

docs.title: Content-Type
docs.text:
Specifies the format of the request body.

Example:

Content-Type: application/json

The API accepts JSON payloads.

docs.title: Accept
docs.text:
Specifies the response format expected by the client.

Example:

Accept: application/json

docs.title: Idempotency-Key
docs.text:
Uniquely identifies a request so that repeated retries do not create duplicate resources.

Example:

Idempotency-Key: 7e4c6f0b-d2c3-4d91-9f6d-0c4f7d8b2a91

Supported only by endpoints that explicitly document idempotency.

docs.title: User-Agent
docs.text:
Identifies the client application making the request.

Example:

User-Agent: SupercardApp/1.0

Providing a meaningful User-Agent assists with diagnostics and operational monitoring.

docs.title: Response Headers
docs.text: The API returns response headers containing metadata about the request and response.

docs.title: Content-Type
docs.text:
Indicates the format of the response body.

Example:

Content-Type: application/json

docs.title: X-Request-ID
docs.text:
Unique identifier assigned to the request.

Example:

X-Request-ID: REQ-20260730-AB12345

Include this identifier when reporting issues or troubleshooting API requests.

docs.title: X-RateLimit-Limit
docs.text:
Maximum number of requests permitted during the current rate limit window.

Example:

X-RateLimit-Limit: 100

docs.title: X-RateLimit-Remaining
docs.text:
Number of requests remaining before the limit is reached.

Example:

X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42

docs.title: X-RateLimit-Reset
docs.text:
Time at which the current rate limit window resets.

Example:

X-RateLimit-Reset: 1722326400

docs.title: Retry-After
docs.text:
Returned when the client exceeds the permitted request rate.

Example:

Retry-After: 60

The value represents the number of seconds the client should wait before retrying.

docs.title: Common Request Example
docs.text:
GET /employees HTTP/1.1
Host: api.supercard.com
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
Accept: application/json
User-Agent: SupercardApp/1.0

docs.title: Common Response Example
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
X-Request-ID: REQ-20260730-AB12345
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 99

docs.title: Header Summary
docs.text:
Header Direction Required Purpose Authorization Request Yes* OAuth 2.0 authentication Content-Type Request When sending a body Indicates request payload format Accept Request Recommended Indicates preferred response format Idempotency-Key Request Conditional Prevents duplicate operations User-Agent Request Recommended Identifies the client application Content-Type Response Yes Indicates response format X-Request-ID Response Yes Unique request identifier X-RateLimit-Limit Response Conditional Maximum requests allowed X-RateLimit-Remaining Response Conditional Remaining requests X-RateLimit-Reset Response Conditional Rate limit reset time Retry-After Response Conditional Delay before retrying

* Authentication is required only for protected endpoints.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always send the Authorization header for protected endpoints.
  • Use application/json for requests and responses.
  • Log the X-Request-ID for troubleshooting.
  • Respect the Retry-After header when present.
  • Provide a descriptive User-Agent for production applications.
